title: Whether The Legal Demand Notice Was ... vs . on 2 May, 2011
full_text: Whether The Legal Demand Notice Was ... vs . on 2 May, 2011 IN THE COURT OF SH.SUSHIL ANUJ TYAGI METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE: DWARKA COURT:NEW DELHI CC No. 9332/09 IN THE MATTER OF M/s D. K. Associates Having its Office at: 38, Devli Road, Khanpur Extn. Near Punjab National Bank New Delhi­110062 ... Complainant. Vs. Sh. Rohtash s/o Sh. Viram Singh r/o B­227, Amritpuri Gali no. 10, Garhi, East of Kailash, New Delhi ... Accused Date of institution of case : 09.01.2009 Date of reserving Judgment : 30.04.2011 Date of pronouncement : 02.05.2011 JUDGMENT 1. Serial No. of the case : 9332/2009 2. Name of the complainant : M/s D. K. Associates 3. Name of the accused : Sh. Rohtash CC No. 9332/09 D.K. Associates Vs. Rohtash Page no. 1/14 4. Offence complained of : S.138 N. I. Act, 1881 5. Plea of accused : Pleaded not guilty. 6. Final Order : Acquitted 7. Date of such order : 02.05.2011 BRIEF FACTS AND REASONS FOR DECISION OF THE CASE 1. This is a complaint under section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act "). 2. The facts of the case as per the complainant are that the accused was granted a loan on 16.10.2007 by the complainant. The accused has issued a cheque bearing no. 210468 dated 22.11.2008 drawn on State Bank of Bikaner & Jaipur for amount of Rs. 95,000, to the complainant towards discharge of liability/debt which got dishonoured on presentation for the reason "Insufficient Funds" vide return memo dated 26.11.2008. The complainant sent legal notice dt. 18.12.2008 to the accused vide Registered post/UPC on 18.12.2008 and despite service the accused did not paid the cheque amount. Hence the present complaint was filed against the accused by the complainant through its authorised representative on 09.01.2009 (hereinafter referred to as "AR"). 3. The AR was examined under section 200 Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter referred to as " CrPC ") by way of tendering of pre­ CC No. 9332/09 D.K. Associates Vs. Rohtash Page no. 2/14 summoning affidavit. 4. After being satisfied that prima facie ingredients of Section 138 NI Act are made out, cognizance was taken and accused was summoned under section 204 CrPC. 5. After appearance of the accused the notice under section 251 CrPC was served on the accused to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 6. In Complainant's evidence, the AR (CW 1) tendered post­ summoning evidence as Ex CW 1/H and relied on documents: Ex CW1/A ­Power of attorney Ex CW1/B ­Cheques in question (colly.) Ex CW1/C ­Return memo Ex CW1/D ­Legal notice Ex CW1/E ­Postal receipt Ex CW1/F ­UPC receipt Ex CW1/G ­Complaint 7. The CW1 was examined, cross­examined and discharged. The Complainant evidence was closed. 8. The accused was examined under section 313 CrPC where all the incriminating evidence was put to the accused. Accused admitted the fact of approaching of complainant by the accused for loan and receiving cash Rs 23000 from the complainant however he denied the issuance of the CC No. 9332/09 D.K. Associates Vs. Rohtash Page no. 3/14 impugned cheque.. Accused raised a defence that the complainant had taken 12 blank signed cheques from him. It was stated that the body of the impugned cheque was not filled by him and he became aware about the present complaint when he received the summons from court.. He denied receiving any notice from the complainant. He wished to lead defence evidence. 9. In defence, accused filed application under section 315 CrPC to examine himself as DW1. DW1 was accordingly examined, cross­ examined and discharged. Defence evidence was closed and the matter was fixed for final arguments. 10. In final arguments, the learned counsel for complainant has submitted that the accused had issued the impugned cheque towards the discharge of legally enforceable liability and he had assured that the it would be duly honoured on presentation. It is further submitted that the accused has also admitted that he had issued the impugned cheque in his disposition. It is alleged that despite service of legal demand notice the accused had not paid the cheque amount within 15 days therefore he had committed the offence u/s 138 NI Act. It is further argued that nothing contradictory has come out in the cross­examination of CW­1 and accused has failed to prove his innocence. It is further submitted that the accused has admitted that he has not paid any EMI towards the loan. It is lastly submitted that the complainant has proved his case beyond doubt CC No. 9332/09 D.K. Associates Vs. Rohtash Page no. 4/14 and the accused be punished as per law. The learned counsel has also submitted written arguments. 11. The learned counsel for the accused, on the other hand, has submitted that the legal demand notice has not been served upon the accused and therefore the case u/s 138 NI Act is not made out. It is argued that the offence is made out only when the notice is served and to support this contention, the learned counsel for the defence has relied on the judgment of Hon'ble Orissa High Court in Markaradhwaj Behera v. Satyanath Mahanta & Anr I (2011) CCR 21. It is averred that the loan amount was not mentioned by the complainant in the complaint and the complainant through this cheque has claimed 95,000/­ from the accused. It is alleged that by no means such a figure can be arrived at by the complainant. It is submitted that even for the sake of arguments if the contention of complainant is accepted that the loan was for Rs. 75,000, the outstanding of Rs. 95,000 cannot be due. The complainant has not filed loan agreement and has also not shown how the liability of Rs. 95,000 exists. It is further submitted that the accused is illiterate and signs in Hindi and the impugned cheque is filled by the complainant on their own whim and fancies. The learned counsel further submitted that the accused had handed over blank cheques to the complainant and the accused had received an amount of Rs. 23,000 in cash from the complainant. It is alleged that the present cheque in question is not issued CC No. 9332/09 D.K. Associates Vs. Rohtash Page no. 5/14 towards any legally enforceable liability or consideration and therefore the accused is entitled to be acquitted. 12. After hearing the arguments and perusal of judicial record, the following questions have levelled up for consideration of this court: 1. Whether the legal demand notice was served upon the accused? 2. Whether the impugned cheques were issued towards legally enforceable debt/liability and consideration? Question no.1 13. In the present case, the legal demand notice as envisaged u/s 138 NI Act is sent by the complainant to the accused through registered post and UPC for which the receipts has been filed on record. No proof of delivery is available on record. The accused has denied receiving any notice from the complainant. Though it is a trite law that sending is not same as receiving of notice and for constituting an offence u/s 138 NI Act, it is sine qua non that the accused must have been served with the legal notice. However, it is not necessary that there should be actual service, the deemed service may also be sufficient for the purposes of S.138 NI Act. The presumption u/s 27 General Clauses Act, 1897 is against the accused. Section 27 General Clauses Act reads: "27. Meaning of service by post. Where any Central Act or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act authorizes or requires any document to be served by post, whether the expression serve or either of the expressions give or send or any other expression is used, then, unless a different intention CC No. 9332/09 D.K. Associates Vs. Rohtash Page no. 6/14 appears, the service shall be deemed to be effected by properly addressing, prepaying and posting by registered post, a letter containing the document, and, unless the contrary is proved, to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post." 14. In C.C. Alavi Haji Appellant v. Palapetty Muhammed & Anr. Respondents 2007 STPL(DC) 952 SC, it was observed: "14. Section 27 gives rise to a presumption that service of notice has been effected when it is sent to the correct address by registered post. In view of the said presumption, when stating that a notice has been sent by registered post to the address of the drawer, it is unnecessary to further aver in the complaint that in spite of the return of the notice unserved, it is deemed to have been served or that the addressee is deemed to have knowledge of the notice. Unless and until the contrary is proved by the addressee, service of notice is deemed to have been effected at the time at which the letter would have been delivered in the ordinary course of business. This Court has already held that when a notice is sent by registered post and is returned with a postal endorsement "refused" or "not available in the house" or "house locked" or "shop closed" or "addressee not in station", due service has to be presumed. [ Vide Jagdish Singh Vs. Natthu Singh , AIR 1992 SC 1604, State of M.P. Vs. Hiralal & Ors. (1996) 7 SCC 523 and V. Raja Kumari Vs. P. Sub­barama Naidu & Anr. (2004) 8 SCC 774]. It is, therefore, manifest that in view of the presumption available under Section 27 of the Act, it is not necessary to aver in the complaint under Section 138 of the Act that service of notice was evaded by the accused or that the accused had a role to play, in the return of the notice unserved." It was further observed: "17. It is also to be borne in mind that the requirement of giving of notice is a clear departure from the rule of Criminal CC No. 9332/09 D.K. Associates Vs. Rohtash Page no. 7/14 Law, where there is no stipulation of giving of a notice before filing a complaint. Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the notice sent by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of sum mons from the court in respect of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, make payment of the cheque amount and submit to the Court that he had made payment within 15 days of receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with the summons) and, therefore, the complaint is liable to be re jected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the Court along with the copy of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required under Section 138 , by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Section 27 of the G.C. Act and Section 114 of the Evidence Act. In our view, any other interpretation of the proviso would defeat the very object of the legislation. As observed in Bhaskaran's case (supra), if the "giving of notice" in the context of Clause (b) of the proviso was the same as the "receipt of notice" a trickster cheque drawer would get the premium to avoid receiving the notice by adopting different strategies and escape from legal consequences of Section 138 of the Act." 15. Thus, it is very clear from S. 27 that when a registered letter is sent to the correct address, it is deemed to be served upon the addressee in the ordinary course. Thus even in absence of the acknowledgment card, the service of legal demand notice is presumed in the present case. S. 27 uses the words "unless the contrary is proved", it means that unless the accused proves by evidence or probabilities to the contrary the service is presumed. The burden was on the accused to rebut the said presumption. The accused had not led any evidence to the contrary and thus has failed CC No. 9332/09 D.K. Associates Vs. Rohtash Page no. 8/14 to rebut the aforesaid presumption. Therefore this court holds that the accused was served with the legal demand notice as envisaged by S.138 NI Act. The judgment Markaradhwaj Behera v. Satyanath Mahanta & Anr (supra) relied upon by the defence is of no benefit to him as the fact of that case totally differ from the present case. In that case, the registered post has received back with the endorsement that the addressee was absent for six to seven days however in the present case the registered post has not received back. Thus the judgment does not find applicability the present case. Question no.2 16. Now, as far as the second question is concerned, it is important to discuss the law relating to Section 138 before proceeding further. Section 138 NI Act reads as under: "138. Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the accounts Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for "a term which may extend to two year", or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless­ (a) The cheque has been presented to the bank within a period CC No. 9332/09 D.K. Associates Vs. Rohtash Page no. 9/14 of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier. (b) The payee or the holder induce course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice, in writing, to the drawer, of the cheque, "within thirty days" of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheques as unpaid, and (c) The drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation: For the purpose of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability." [Emphasis added] 17. The NI Act raises a rebuttable presumption under section 139 NI Act and 118 NI Act against the accused and in favour of the holder of cheque. 18. Section 139 NI Act reads: "139. Presumption in favour of holder It shall be presumed, unless the Contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, or any debt or other liability." [Emphasis added] Section 118 NI Act reads: "118. Presumptions as to negotiable instruments of consideration Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made: ­ (h) Of consideration: that every negotiable instrument CC No. 9332/09 D.K. Associates Vs. Rohtash Page no. 10/14 was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has bee accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration. ........................................................................" [Emphasis added] 19. The accused may rebut the presumptions u/s 139 NI Act & u/s 118 NI Act by leading evidence or by showing preponderance of probabilities. In Rangappa v. Sri Mohan 2010 STPL(DC) 952 SC, it was observed: "14.................................However, it must be remembered that the offence made punishable by Section 138 can be better described as a regulatory offence since the bouncing of a cheque is largely in the nature of a civil wrong whose impact is usually confined to the private parties involved in commercial transactions. In such a scenario, the test of proportionality should guide the construction and interpretation of reverse onus clauses and the accused/ defendant cannot be expected to discharge an unduly high standard or proof. In the absence of compelling justifications, reverse onus clauses usually impose an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. Keeping this in view, it is a settled position that when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of' preponderance of probabilities'. Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable CC No. 9332/09 D.K. Associates Vs. Rohtash Page no. 11/14 defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. As clarified in the citations, the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own." 20. In the present case, the complainant had averred in the complaint that the accused had taken a loan however no loan amount was mentioned therein. During the cross­examination of CW­1, CW­1 expressed his lack of knowledge about the how much amount was demanded by the accused as loan from the complainant. The CW­1 deposed that the accused was granted a loan of Rs. 75,000 however, he could not state on being questioned as to how the loan amount was paid to the accused. The complainant has not proved how much amount was given to the accused as loan and by what mode the amount was paid to the accused. This raises a considerable doubt on the loan amount. CW­1 denied the suggestion that Rs. 23,000 in cash were paid to the accused as loan amount. The loan agreement was not proved by the complainant in the present case. The accused has examined himself as DW­1 and has deposed clearly with dates that he had received in cash Rs. 17,000 on 16.10.2007 and Rs. 6,000 on 09.11.2007. The accused was cross­ examined by the learned counsel for the complainant but he could not extract anything to prove the prosecution case. Though the accused has CC No. 9332/09 D.K. Associates Vs. Rohtash Page no. 12/14 stated during cross examination that he did not paid any amount towards the loan, however at the same time, this is clarified by the accused that since the accused had not received the full loan amount he did not paid the EMI. In these circumstances, the burden of proof has reverted back on the complainant and it is proper for this court to conclude that the complainant has not proved the legally enforceable liability or debt against the accused. 21. In the present case, the cheque amount is 95,000 and even if it is accepted that the loan was for Rs. 75,000 there is nothing proved on record to show how this liability of Rs. 75,000 has raised to Rs.95,000 for which the impugned cheque was drawn. Also, the accused has accepted his signatures on the cheque which are in Hindi and rest of the body on the cheque is filled in English with different ink, this fact also supports the defence version that the cheque was handed over as blank to the complainant. The complainant has also not proved how the cheque was issued by the accused and whether it was towards some settlement arrived at between the parties. These circumstances has created serious dents in the prosecution story. 22. In view of these discussions and observations, this court has no hesitation to conclude that the accused has successfully rebutted the presumption that the impugned cheques were issued for consideration under section 118 NI or that the impugned cheques were issued towards CC No. 9332/09 D.K. Associates Vs. Rohtash Page no. 13/14 legally enforceable liability or debt under section 139 NI Act. FINAL ORDER 23. In view of above discussions and observations, this court holds that the complainant has failed to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt against the accused. 24. This court acquits the accused Rohtash for the offence under section 138 NI Act. Bail bonds are cancelled and sureties, if any, are discharged. 25. File be consigned to Record Room. Announced in the open Court on 02.05.2011 (Sushil Anuj Tyagi) Metropolitan Magistrate Dwarka, New Delhi 02.05.2011 CC No. 9332/09 D.K. Associates Vs. Rohtash Page no. 14/14
